# About

URL: https://kompositenews.com/about/

About Komposite News
Komposite News is an independent digital publication covering artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital assets, enterprise technology, cybersecurity, fintech and capital markets. We write for executives, founders, investors, developers and policy professionals who need to understand how technology and finance are changing each other.
Our coverage prioritizes reporting and analysis over hype. We are interested in what is being built, what it costs, who is buying it and what the consequences are, and we hold breathless claims from any direction to the same standard of evidence.
Komposite News is edited and published by Cory Chamberlain.
Ownership and funding: Komposite News is independently operated. Any commercial relationship relevant to a story is disclosed within that story, and sponsored content is always clearly labeled. Questions about the publication can be directed through our contact page.

# Editorial Standards

URL: https://kompositenews.com/editorial-standards/

Editorial Standards
Komposite News reports facts we can verify and clearly distinguishes reporting from analysis and opinion. News stories describe what happened. Pieces labeled Analysis interpret events and draw conclusions from evidence. Pieces labeled Opinion argue a point of view and represent their author.
We attribute information to sources wherever possible, grant anonymity only when information is significant and cannot otherwise be obtained, and independently verify claims before publishing them. We do not accept payment for editorial coverage, and staff may not trade on non-public information obtained through reporting.
Sponsored or partner content, when it appears, is labeled unambiguously and is never presented in editorial form without that label. Errors, when they occur, are corrected promptly and transparently under our corrections policy.
How we use AI
AI at Komposite News. Komposite uses AI tools to summarise filings, regulatory notices and company statements, to draft articles and to translate some Spanish-language pages. From November 2026 onward, no article goes up until a human editor has approved it.
Stories without an individual author carry the Komposite News Staff byline. Corrections: contact the newsroom via our contact page with the article link and the specific claim at issue, as set out in our corrections policy.

# AI Policy

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai-policy/

AI Policy
AI at Komposite News. Komposite uses AI tools to summarise filings, regulatory notices and company statements, to draft articles and to translate some Spanish-language pages. From November 2026 onward, no article goes up until a human editor has approved it.
Stories without an individual author carry the Komposite News Staff byline. AI tools also help with site infrastructure.
Quotes are published only when we can match them to a source or the person approved them. We do not publish AI-generated statements attributed to real people, AI-fabricated data, or synthetic imagery presented as photography. Illustrations are labeled as illustrations, photographs carry credits and licenses, and sample or demonstration data is labeled as such wherever it appears.
This policy will evolve with the technology. Questions about how a specific story was produced can be directed to the newsroom via our contact page.

# What buyers actually do with an SBOM

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/sbom-what-buyers-do-with-it/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-30T09:00:00Z

Software bills of materials are now routinely produced and routinely ignored, and the gap between generating one and acting on it is where the risk sits.

The argument about whether vendors should produce a software bill of materials is over. Vendors produce them. The interesting question, and the one procurement teams are least prepared for, is what happens to the file after it arrives.
An SBOM is an inventory: the components inside a piece of software, their versions, and their relationships to one another. Its value is entirely conditional. It answers one question well, which is whether a newly disclosed vulnerability is present in something already installed, and it answers that question only if somebody is holding it when the disclosure lands.
The baseline moved this year. American authorities published an updated set of minimum elements, replacing guidance that had stood since the original executive order and raising what a compliant document is expected to contain.
That update matters more than it sounds, because the minimum elements are what contracts point at. A purchase order rarely specifies a format in detail. It references a standard, and the standard quietly determines how much work a vendor has to do.
Adoption across the European market has been surveyed rather than assumed. The EU cybersecurity agency's review of where SBOM practice actually stands describes an ecosystem where generation is increasingly routine and consumption remains the weak link.
That asymmetry is the whole story. Producing an SBOM is a build-pipeline problem, and build pipelines are the part of software organizations most amenable to automation. Consuming one is an operations problem, and operations teams are already the most oversubscribed function in most security programs.
The result is a familiar organizational pattern. A file arrives, satisfies a contractual requirement, and is stored where nothing queries it. The obligation is met and the risk is unchanged, which is the worst of both outcomes because it also produces a record showing the buyer was told.
Teams that get value from the practice describe the same prerequisite, and it is not tooling. It is knowing what software they run, at which version, in which environment, well enough to join that list against an inventory. Organizations that cannot answer the first question gain nothing from the second.
Regulatory drivers keep expanding the population who must care. Medical device guidance, the European cyber resilience regime and federal procurement terms each require the artifact in their own context, and each has a different theory of what the recipient is supposed to do with it.
Practitioners are candid that the honest use case is narrower than the marketing. When a widely used component is found to be catastrophically vulnerable, an SBOM turns a week of frantic archaeology into a database query. Between those events it is a maintenance cost.
That is a reasonable trade and a smaller claim than the one usually made for it. The organizations doing this well are not the ones with the best-formatted files. They are the ones who can answer, on the afternoon the disclosure lands, where the affected component is running.

# What an attestation must prove

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/what-an-attestation-must-prove/
Section: Crypto
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-09-03T14:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-09-03T14:00:00Z

Stablecoin law requires monthly examination of reserves, and the open rulemaking question is what level of assurance that examination must actually deliver.

The argument about whether stablecoin issuers should publish their reserves is finished. Federal law requires it. The argument that replaced it is narrower, more technical, and determines whether the requirement means very much: what an examination of those reserves has to establish.
The statute sets the frame. The GENIUS Act requires permitted issuers to publish the composition of their reserves monthly, to have those reports examined by a registered public accounting firm, and to obtain certifications from the chief executive and chief financial officer.
Monthly is a demanding cadence for anything an accounting firm signs. Most public company reporting is quarterly with a single annual audit, so the law is asking for a recurring procedure that has no exact precedent at this frequency.
The open question is the assurance level, and it is not a technicality. An examination performed at limited assurance concludes that nothing came to the practitioner's attention suggesting a problem. One performed at reasonable assurance states positively that the reserves are what the issuer says they are.
Those are different products with different costs and very different meanings to a reader, and the same document title can describe either. A holder comparing two issuers' monthly reports has no reliable way to tell which standard produced them without reading the fine print.
Regulators are consulting rather than assuming. Rulemaking has asked directly whether the examination should be conducted at reasonable assurance, under established attestation standards, or under an alternative framework built for the purpose.
The content of the disclosure is comparatively settled. The expected reporting covers the par value of coins outstanding, the fair value of reserve assets by category, the weighted average maturity of Treasury holdings, the names of custodians and depository institutions, and a reconciliation showing reserves at least equal outstanding coins.
That reconciliation is the heart of it. Everything else describes the portfolio; the reconciliation is the statement that the portfolio covers the liability, and it is the sentence a holder is actually relying on when they treat a token as a dollar.
Supervisors have published implementation requirements through the ordinary rulemaking process, including standards for insured depository institutions and supervised issuers, which is how a novel instrument gets absorbed into an existing supervisory apparatus.
The practical effect of a strong answer would be consolidation. A monthly reasonable-assurance examination is expensive, requires reserve assets an accounting firm can verify quickly, and is easiest for issuers holding short Treasuries at large custodians, which is a narrower field than the one that exists today.
That may be the intended outcome. A payment instrument that circulates as a dollar substitute is a poor place for structural creativity, and the assurance standard is the lever that decides how much of it survives.

# What a seed round now requires

URL: https://kompositenews.com/startups/what-a-seed-round-now-requires/
Section: Startups
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-08-27T09:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-27T09:00:00Z

Seed rounds now arrive after revenue and retention evidence that once belonged to Series A, and the gap between rounds has stretched past two years.

The seed round kept its name and quietly changed its meaning. What investors now expect before writing that check is roughly what a Series A required a few years ago, and founders planning against the old definition run out of money at the point they expected to raise.
The clearest expression of the shift is time. Data assembled from company cap tables shows the interval between rounds stretching well past two years, which means a seed round is no longer bridging to a nearby milestone. It has to fund the company to a materially different business.
That arithmetic changes how much to raise and what to promise. A round sized for eighteen months against a market that now takes twenty-four produces a company that is technically alive and practically unfundable, holding a deck full of progress and a bank balance that ends the conversation.
Investors describe the bar in terms of evidence rather than vision. Revenue that recurs, retention that survives a renewal cycle, and unit economics the founder can explain without a chart have replaced the narrative rounds that characterized the last cycle.
Pre-seed absorbed the difference. What used to be called seed is now a distinct earlier stage with its own norms and its own investors, which means the ladder gained a rung rather than losing one, and the founder climbs the same distance in more steps.
Formation costs falling has made this possible without making it pleasant. Building a credible product is cheaper than it has ever been, so the evidence investors demand is now genuinely obtainable before a round, which is precisely why it is demanded.
The concentration of capital into a narrow band of companies compounds the effect. When most of a fund's deployment goes to a small number of category-defining bets, the diligence applied to everything else tightens, because those checks have to clear a higher internal bar to justify the attention.
Founders who have raised recently describe the practical adaptation as unglamorous. Charge earlier than feels comfortable, treat the first ten paying customers as the fundraise rather than as a precursor to it, and keep the burn low enough that the round is optional for a quarter longer than planned.
The uncomfortable part is what this selects for. Requiring commercial evidence before capital favors founders who can survive unpaid for longer, which is a filter on personal circumstances as much as on ability, and the industry has not found a good answer to that.
Investors are candid that the discipline is real and its distribution is not. The companies that clear the new bar are unquestionably stronger at the same stage than their predecessors, and some number of good companies never got far enough to be measured.
The stage will keep its name regardless. It is worth understanding that the word now describes a company with customers, and planning the eighteen months before it accordingly.

# AI in the order flow: what machine trading is doing to volatility

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/volatility-market-structure-ai-trading/
Section: Markets
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-07-17T15:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-17T15:00:00Z

Adaptive execution and model-driven strategies are changing intraday dynamics in ways researchers are only beginning to measure.

Machine learning has been in markets for years, but the current generation of adaptive execution and model-driven strategies behaves differently from its rule-based ancestors, and researchers are working out what that means for volatility itself.
Early findings are mixed in instructive ways. Adaptive strategies appear to dampen volatility in normal conditions, adjusting quickly to absorb flow imbalances, while contributing to sharper moves when many models respond to the same signal simultaneously. Calm most days, and a faster crowd on the days that matter.
Regulators are asking measurement questions before policy ones: how much flow is model-driven, how correlated are the models, and whether existing circuit breakers match the speed of the herding they are meant to interrupt. Exchanges, holding the data, have become reluctant referees in the debate.
RelatedDigital asset market making becomes an institutional business ›Practitioners mostly shrug at the framing. Every generation of market technology, they note, was accused of breaking volatility until it became the baseline against which the next generation was accused. The honest answer is that the market is running the experiment on itself, and the results publish in real time.

# Machine identity sprawl becomes security's biggest inventory problem

URL: https://kompositenews.com/cybersecurity/identity-machine-workloads/
Section: Cybersecurity
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-07-10T10:55:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-10T10:55:00Z

Service accounts, API keys, and agent credentials now outnumber human identities many times over, and governance is racing the growth.

For every human identity in a modern enterprise there are many machine ones, service accounts, API keys, certificates, and now AI agent credentials, and most organizations cannot count them, let alone govern them. Machine identity has become the inventory problem that defines the next phase of identity security.
The risk profile is distinctive: machine credentials are long-lived, widely copied, and rarely owned by anyone who remembers creating them. Incident reviews repeatedly trace breaches to forgotten service accounts with standing privileges, and the remediation is lifecycle discipline, issuance, rotation, expiry, applied at a scale human identity never required.
RelatedCybersecurity spending shifts toward identity and resilience ›Agentic AI raised the stakes by adding credentials that act autonomously. The emerging standard treats every agent as a governed identity with scoped permissions and an accountable human sponsor, which is less a new idea than the old one, finally enforced on the population that grew fastest.

# Enterprises write the rulebook for AI-generated code

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/ai-coding-tools-enterprise-standards/
Section: AI
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-06-26T13:30:00Z
Updated: 2026-06-26T13:30:00Z

Provenance tracking, review gates, and dependency policies are turning AI coding assistance from a developer perk into governed infrastructure.

AI coding assistants arrived in enterprises through developer enthusiasm and settled in ahead of policy. The policy is now catching up. Engineering organizations are formalizing rules for machine-generated code: what must be tracked, what must be reviewed differently, and what may not be generated at all.
Provenance is the anchor requirement. Compliance teams want to know which code a model wrote, which model wrote it, and what the model was shown, both for license exposure and for the audits that regulated industries already face. Tooling vendors have responded with attribution tracking that engineering leaders describe as necessary and nobody describes as finished.
RelatedAI infrastructure spending moves into a new phase ›The practical effect on productivity has been smaller than skeptics predicted. Teams report that governance slowed adoption for a quarter and then became routine, the same arc that source control and code review followed in earlier decades. The tools stayed; the anarchy did not.

# AI evaluation grows from afterthought to budget line

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/ai-evaluation-becomes-budget-line/
Section: AI
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-08-05T13:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-05T13:40:00Z

Enterprises deploying models at scale are formalizing evaluation the way they once formalized QA, and a vendor category is forming around it.

When AI systems were pilots, evaluation was a spreadsheet. Now that they process claims, answer customers, and draft contracts, companies are treating evaluation as standing infrastructure, with dedicated staff, tooling budgets, and sign-off authority over releases.
The change is driven less by regulation than by incident reports. Organizations that shipped model updates without regression testing describe the same experience: a quiet degradation in some workflow no one was watching, discovered by customers rather than dashboards. Formal evaluation pipelines are the institutional response.
A market is forming to serve the need. Startups sell evaluation harnesses, scored datasets tailored to industries, and monitoring that flags drift in production. Incumbent observability vendors are extending into the category, arguing that model behavior is simply another production signal.
RelatedEnterprise buyers push for clearer AI contract terms ›The maturity marker executives cite is procedural: whether a model change can be blocked. In organizations where evaluation owns a veto, the function is real. Where it produces reports no one must read, it remains a spreadsheet with a bigger budget.

# Power availability becomes the master constraint on computing

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/power-constraints-shape-computing/
Section: Technology
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-07-27T09:15:00Z
Updated: 2026-07-27T09:15:00Z

Grid interconnection queues, not chip supply, now set the timeline for new capacity, and the industry is reorganizing around electrons.

Ask data center developers what gates their next project and the answer is no longer silicon. It is the interconnection queue, the multi-year wait for utility approval to draw large amounts of power from grids that were not planned for computing's growth curve.
The constraint is reorganizing the industry's geography and structure. Development migrates to regions with spare generation and faster approvals; operators contract directly for new generation, sometimes co-developing it; and a market has emerged in sites whose chief asset is a signed interconnection agreement.
On-site and adjacent generation has moved from contingency to strategy. Gas turbines as bridge power, long-term contracts anchoring new renewable buildouts, and serious capital behind small modular nuclear all reflect the same conclusion: waiting for the grid is the expensive option.
RelatedLiquid cooling stops being optional in AI data centers ›The policy dimension is unavoidable. Computing's power demand lands on ratepayers, regulators, and climate commitments simultaneously, and jurisdictions are diverging on who pays for the upgrades and who gets priority in the queue. Where those questions get answered favorably is, increasingly, where the next generation of infrastructure gets built.

# Shadow AI becomes the new shadow IT

URL: https://kompositenews.com/business/shadow-ai-governance-problem/
Section: Business
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-08-07T11:25:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-07T11:25:00Z

Employees are routing work through unsanctioned AI tools faster than policies can name them, and enterprises are choosing between control and visibility.

Every technology wave produces its shadow, and AI's arrived on schedule. Employees across functions are routing drafting, analysis, and coding through personal accounts on consumer AI tools, outside procurement, outside logging, and outside whatever policy the company wrote last quarter.
The governance instinct is prohibition, and the operational evidence is that prohibition fails quietly. Organizations that blocked consumer tools report usage migrating to personal devices, trading visible risk for invisible risk. The emerging alternative is substitution: sanctioned tools good enough that the shadow versions lose their appeal, paired with monitoring that treats AI traffic like any other data flow.
RelatedEnterprise software pricing strains under the weight of AI ›Security leaders describe the moment in familiar terms, because they lived it with cloud storage and messaging apps. The lesson they cite from those episodes is consistent: the workforce adopts what works, and governance succeeds by arriving with a better answer rather than a longer denial.

# Instant payments become table stakes in B2B

URL: https://kompositenews.com/fintech/instant-payments-b2b-standard/
Section: Fintech
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-08-12T11:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-08-12T11:20:00Z

Real-time rails are moving from consumer novelty to supplier expectation, and the software layer on top is where the margin lives.

Instant payment rails, built for consumers splitting dinner, are being colonized by business finance. Supplier payments, insurance disbursements, and payroll adjustments increasingly ride real-time systems, and the expectation is spreading through supply chains faster than the infrastructure teams behind it anticipated.
The shift exposes where the value actually sits. Moving money instantly is becoming a commodity; knowing why it moved is not. The software that attaches invoices, remittance data, and reconciliation to real-time payments commands the margin the rails themselves are losing.
Corporate adoption follows a practical script: start with the payments where speed is worth money, urgent supplier releases, claim payouts, final payrolls, then expand as finance teams trust the controls. Fraud tooling has had to accelerate in parallel, since irrevocable and instant is a demanding combination.
RelatedWhen software spends: payments build an authorization layer for AI agents ›Banks find themselves both essential and squeezed, operating the rails while fintech intermediaries own the customer experience above them. The competitive response, embedding payment capabilities directly into the software businesses already use, is reshaping bank product organizations around a fact they long resisted: the interface is the relationship.

# Stablecoin Reserve reporting converges on common standards

URL: https://kompositenews.com/crypto/stablecoin-reserve-transparency-standards/
Section: Crypto
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-03-06T08:45:00Z
Updated: 2026-03-06T08:45:00Z

Monthly attestations are giving way to standardized disclosures that let treasurers compare issuers the way they compare money market funds.

Stablecoin issuers are learning to speak the language of money market funds. Reserve disclosures, once a patchwork of voluntary attestations in incompatible formats, are converging on standardized reporting of composition, maturity, and counterparties, driven by regulation in some jurisdictions and competitive pressure everywhere else.
The audience is corporate. Treasurers evaluating stablecoins for payments want the same visibility they get from a fund fact sheet, and issuers courting that demand have discovered that transparency is a product feature. Disclosure quality now appears in payment providers' issuer scorecards alongside redemption terms.
Standardization enables comparison, and comparison disciplines behavior. Analysts publishing side-by-side reserve breakdowns note measurable shifts toward shorter maturities and simpler holdings since standard formats took hold, the market rewarding conservatism it can finally see.
RelatedStablecoin law meets its implementation year ›Gaps remain, particularly in real-time reporting and the treatment of reserves held across borders. But the direction is set, and it points toward stablecoins being evaluated with the tools of cash management rather than the vocabulary of crypto.

# Interoperability standards take shape for institutional chains

URL: https://kompositenews.com/blockchain/interoperability-standards-institutional-chains/
Section: Blockchain
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2025-11-12T10:05:00Z
Updated: 2025-11-12T10:05:00Z

Messaging standards bodies and blockchain consortia are converging on formats that let regulated ledgers talk to each other, and to the systems banks already run.

The institutional blockchain world is discovering what payments learned decades ago: networks that cannot interoperate stay small. Standards work, unfashionable and slow, has become the venue where the next phase of adoption is actually being decided.
The convergence underway joins two traditions. Financial messaging bodies bring the discipline of standardized data formats that banks already parse, while blockchain consortia bring transfer protocols proven on public networks. The emerging designs let a tokenized asset move between regulated ledgers while carrying the structured information compliance systems require.
Progress is measured in pilots that would once have been impossible: assets issued on one institution's ledger settling against payment on another's, with both sides reconciled automatically. Participants emphasize that none of it required the institutions to share a chain, only a vocabulary.
RelatedBanks test blockchain settlement without abandoning existing rails ›The stakes are consolidation versus fragmentation. If common standards hold, tokenized markets can scale across institutions the way correspondent banking did. If they fail, each network remains an island, and the efficiency case for the technology weakens accordingly.

# Chase blames a bug, and the outage rule counts bugs

URL: https://kompositenews.com/fintech/chase-blames-a-bug-and-the-outage-rule-counts-bugs/
Section: Fintech
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-11-17T14:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-17T14:20:00Z

Chase blamed a bug in on-premise hardware for its 16 Nov outage; the 2021 bank notice rule covers incidents 'from whatever cause', with 36 hours to report.

JPMorgan Chase blamed a software bug in its own on-premise hardware for Monday's disruption to consumer transactions, which customers first reported at about 11:30 EST and which the bank said had cleared by about 18:30 EST.
The largest US bank said in a statement reported by CNBC that it had experienced a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems", that customers could still reach their accounts and funds, and that there was "no evidence it is cyber-related". "This is not a systemic issue," a spokesperson said. Transactions with other banks were delayed only where Chase was a party, the bank said. It has not said how many customers were affected or which system failed.
By about 18:30 a spokesperson told NBC News: "Transactions are now posting normally." Zelle, the payments network operated by Early Warning Services, said: "Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should." U.S. Bank said it was "not directly impacted", PNC was "not experiencing any direct impact" and Capital One "has not been impacted", NBC reported. Bank of America and Citigroup reported no problems with their own services, the Associated Press reported, and some Chase customers saw a message that services were unavailable.
Komposite's timeline from the reports linked in each row. The last row is our arithmetic, not a known filing: the rule's 36 hours run from the moment a bank determines that an incident qualifies, which may be later than the first customer report, and Chase has not said whether or when it made that determination.Time (EST)What happenedHours after first reports
11:30 Mon 16 NovEarliest customer reports of errors, according to CNBC0
About 16:00Chase posts on X that it is working to resolve a temporary issue, NBC News reported4.5
16:41CNBC publishes the bank's statement blaming a software bug in on-premise hardware5.2
About 18:30A spokesperson says "Transactions are now posting normally"7.0
23:30 Tue 17 NovLatest time the OCC could receive notice if Chase had judged at 11:30 on Monday that the outage was a notification incident36.0
Does an outage that is not a cyberattack have to be reported?
It can be. The test in federal banking rules turns on the effect of an incident, not on whether anyone attacked the bank. The computer-security incident notification rule adopted in November 2021 by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Reserve and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, in force since April 2022, defines a computer-security incident as "an occurrence that results in actual harm to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system". The agencies wrote that such incidents "can result from destructive malware or malicious software (cyberattacks), as well as non-malicious failure of hardware and software, personnel errors, and other causes". When two commenters asked them to exclude non-malicious causes, they declined: "For clarity, the definition includes incidents from whatever cause."
An incident becomes reportable, a "notification incident", when it has materially disrupted or degraded, or is reasonably likely to, a bank's ability "to deliver banking products and services to a material portion of its customer base, in the ordinary course of business", or a business line or operations whose failure would threaten financial stability. The agencies listed examples. Two sit close to Monday's facts: "A failed system upgrade or change that results in widespread user outages for customers and banking organization employees", and attacks that "disrupt customer account access for an extended period of time (e.g., more than 4 hours)". Whether Chase's bug met the materiality test is a judgment for the bank and its supervisors; Chase's own statement that customers kept access to their funds would weigh in that judgment.
The deadline is short. A bank "must notify" its primary federal regulator "as soon as possible and no later than 36 hours after the banking organization determines that a notification incident has occurred". For JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., a national bank, that regulator is the OCC; the Fed's version of the rule covers bank holding companies such as JPMorgan Chase & Co. The notice can be an email or a phone call, and "No specific information is required in the notification other than that a notification incident has occurred." Notices are covered by the agencies' confidentiality rules, so if Chase filed one, the public is unlikely to see it.
Banks argued for longer when the rule was drafted. Several commenters asked for 72 hours, to match New York's financial regulator and the EU's data-protection law, and one asked for five business days for banks under $20bn in assets. The agencies kept 36: "The agencies continue to believe that 36 hours is the appropriate timeframe, given the simplicity of the notification requirement and the severity of incidents captured by the definition of 'notification incident.'" They added that the clock starts only once a bank has determined that an incident qualifies, which leaves the bank time to assess what happened.
Komposite's close reading of the final rule, 86 FR 66424, set against the bank's statements as reported by CNBC, NBC News and the AP. The rule's examples are illustrative; each bank decides case by case.What the 2021 rule looks atWhat the rule saysWhat Chase has said in public

How big is the operation that slowed?
Very. JPMorgan Chase held $2.78tn of deposits at 30 September, according to its filings with the SEC, up 8.7 per cent in nine months by our arithmetic. Its spending on technology has grown faster than its other costs. In the first nine months of 2026 the bank's technology, communications and equipment expense was $9.46bn, up 16.5 per cent on a year earlier, while total noninterest expense rose 13.7 per cent.
From the income statement in JPMorgan Chase's 10-Q for the quarter to 30 September 2026 (XBRL rendering). Changes and shares are Komposite's arithmetic.JPMorgan Chase, $ millionsQ3 2025Q3 2026Nine months 2025Nine months 2026Change, nine months

The phrase "on-premise" places the fault in hardware the bank runs itself, rather than with a cloud provider or an outside processor. Chase has not elaborated. Its only Form 8-K on Tuesday, filed with the SEC, concerned the succession of its chief financial officer: Bregje de Best will succeed Jeremy Barnum after the bank reports first-quarter 2027 results, and Barnum will become a vice chairman. It does not mention Monday's outage.
Why it matters
The rule was written for exactly this kind of week. When it was adopted, the agencies estimated about 150 notification incidents a year across the banks they supervise, a figure based on supervisory data and suspicious-activity reports for 2019 and 2020. It also requires vendors that run services for banks to warn their bank customers when a disruption lasts four hours or more. Monday's outage came four days after a Microsoft gateway failure that Microsoft also traced to a latent software defect, and three days after an air traffic control outage that grounded US flights for several hours, the AP noted.
Chase has said its systems are back to normal. What it has not said, how many customers were hit, whether fees or failed payments will be reversed, and whether it judged the outage reportable, is the next thing to watch. Komposite reported in October on JPMorgan's deposit token moving onto Ethereum, part of the same bank's effort to run more of its payments on new rails.

# Microsoft traces its mail outage to a July fix

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/microsoft-traces-its-mail-outage-to-a-july-fix/
Section: Technology
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-11-17T14:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-17T14:00:00Z

Microsoft's preliminary report blames a July Windows fix for the 12-13 Nov Exchange Online outage; over 80% of gateway servers stopped responding.

A Windows fix that Microsoft began deploying in July caused the Exchange Online outage of 12 and 13 November, the company says in a preliminary post-incident report dated 15 November.
A surge of Teams traffic and a block of servers already out of service pushed the gateway in front of Exchange past breaking point, the report says. More than 80 per cent of the gateway's servers stopped responding at the worst point, and mail access was disrupted for most users for 23 hours and 50 minutes.
The seven-page report, a copy of which was published by the Microsoft 365 site 365Fanatic, describes "a latent defect" that made Windows servers "overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions" through "lock contention inside an internal Windows process". The fix was "prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers", and Microsoft says "neither the underlying defect nor the fix applies to broader Windows deployments". The report gives the outage as 16:20 UTC on Thursday to 16:10 UTC on Friday, 23 hours and 50 minutes by our arithmetic.
Why did a July change fail in November?
Because the load changed. The report says the change "first started deployment in July of this year" and that "For more than three months, the change was deployed worldwide without impact", between 104 and 134 days by our count depending on the July start. Load testing missed it: "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores."
Two things then lined up. About 15 hours before the outage, at 01:07 UTC, Teams failed over from Microsoft's alternative gateway onto the "primary" one that also carries Exchange Online, which the report calls "part of normal operations". And "nearly 14% of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service due to an unrelated issue from the previous day". The servers began failing "during the peak window of traffic in the United States". When failing servers handed their traffic to healthy ones, those failed too: "In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet", and "At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive."
Times from Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report, dated 15 November 2026; elapsed hours are Komposite's arithmetic.Time (UTC)What Microsoft's preliminary report says happenedHours after the 16:20 alert
01:07 Thu 12 NovAutomated failover moves Teams traffic onto the gateway servers shared with Exchange Online&minus;15.2
16:03Anomaly monitor sees connectivity problems rising&minus;0.3
16:20High-priority alert; incident EX1550543 posted0
19:00All deployments and configuration changes paused2.7
00:30 Fri 13 NovConnection negotiation identified as the main cause of access failures8.2
07:20Update reverting the defective change applied to part of the capacity15.0
14:17Global webmail availability back to expected levels22.0
16:10No active customer impact; extended monitoring begins23.8
The gateway was built to contain this kind of failure, and that did not work either. Microsoft says the gateway is made of "thousands of 'capacity units'" grouped into regions, but "due to a separate issue, the normal bulkheads between these different partitions did not stop the cascading failure", which is how the fault spread worldwide. The timeline shows the first night's fixes failing: at 22:00 UTC on Thursday Microsoft's telemetry "confirmed that the actions we'd taken to restore service had not been effective", and at 23:55 it found that servers returned to service "initially remained healthy but then become unresponsive again upon receiving traffic". The report does not describe the separate issue that weakened the bulkheads.
Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint moved off the faulty gateway, which is why they recovered first, but "not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons". Restarted servers were "immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic", and because the defect was months old, "our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change". Engineers took eight hours and ten minutes from the first alert to identify connection negotiation as the problem, and 15 hours to begin applying an update that put the code back to its earlier state, by our arithmetic from the report's timeline.
Which start time is right?
The report says 16:20 UTC, but Microsoft's own incident record still disagrees. The closed record for EX1550543, as copied by the University of Pennsylvania on Tuesday, carries a Start Time field of 10:05 UTC, the time Komposite reported on Saturday as a six-hour revision. Its final status text and the report both say 16:20. The record's status changed to "postIncidentReviewPublished" with a note at 04:47 UTC on Monday that "A post-incident report has been published".
Komposite's comparison of Microsoft's service-health record as copied by the University of Pennsylvania with the preliminary report. Uptime is our arithmetic on 43,200 minutes; all three fall in the same credit tier of Microsoft's service-level agreement (below 99 per cent, above 95).Where the start time appearsStart (UTC, Thu 12 Nov)Outage to 16:10 FriUptime for a user out throughout, 30-day month
Incident record as first logged (our 13 November reading)16:1723h53m96.68%
Start Time field of the closed record, still shown on 17 November10:0530h05m95.82%
Final status text and preliminary report16:2023h50m96.69%
For customers' service credits the difference does not change the tier, by our arithmetic, though it changes the minutes counted, which Microsoft measures per user across a tenant. As we reported on Friday, customers have to claim those credits from Microsoft; they are not paid automatically.
The report lists five repair items as completed, including guardrails "for traffic distribution to avoid cascading impact" and more monitoring, and says a "comprehensive list of repair items will be delivered as part of the final PIR" on 20 November, the date The Register also gave. 365Fanatic's summary says the report runs to seven pages. The final report is the next fixed date, five business days after Friday's end time.

# The SEC moves to retire 'compensation actually paid'

URL: https://kompositenews.com/policy/the-sec-moves-to-retire-compensation-actually-paid/
Section: Policy
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-11-17T13:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-17T13:40:00Z

The SEC would replace 'compensation actually paid'; across 1,346 firms it differed from reported CEO pay by a median 37% in fiscal 2025, our analysis finds.

The Securities and Exchange Commission has proposed scrapping "compensation actually paid", a pay measure that differed from reported chief executive pay by a median 37 per cent across 1,346 companies last year, by our analysis.
The proposal, announced on Friday 13 November, would rewrite Item 402 of Regulation S-K, the rule that sets what goes in the pay section of proxy statements. The SEC said the rule was last comprehensively reformed in 2006. Chairman Paul Atkins said in a statement that "the rule has become bloated—reaching nearly the end of the alphabet in its internal organizational system" and that the changes "aim to reduce compliance burdens for companies while remaining faithful to the congressional mandate". Comments are open for 60 days after the proposal appears in the Federal Register; it had not appeared there as of Tuesday, by our check.
What is "compensation actually paid"?
It is the pay-versus-performance figure the SEC created in 2022 to meet a Dodd-Frank Act requirement. It adjusts the summary-table total by replacing the grant-date value of equity awards with their fair value at year-end and changes in that value, so it moves with the share price and can turn negative. Under the proposal, the fact sheet says, the measure would be replaced "with the total amount shown in the Earned Compensation Table", performance disclosure would be limited to cumulative shareholder return, and three years would be shown instead of five.
Companies tag both numbers in their filings, so the gap can be measured. Komposite pulled the SEC's XBRL frames for the 2025 calendar-year period, matched each company's chief executive summary-table total with its compensation actually paid, and kept the 1,346 companies with both. The median company reported $4.40m in its summary table and $3.25m actually paid. Only about a quarter had the two within 10 per cent of each other. The 1,346 are the companies whose filings tag a single chief executive figure for the period, so the count covers most, not all, of the companies that file pay-versus-performance tables; 1,071 of them have fiscal years ending in December.
Komposite's analysis of the chief executive figures that 1,346 companies tagged in their pay-versus-performance tables for fiscal years ending between June 2025 and May 2026, from the SEC's XBRL frames for summary-table total pay and compensation actually paid. Companies with more than one chief executive in the year, which tag each separately, are not in these frames. Medians: $4.40m reported, $3.25m actually paid. Some filers' tags contain obvious scale errors, which is why we use counts and medians rather than totals.How far 'actually paid' sat from the summary-table total, fiscal 2025CompaniesShare
Within 10 per cent either way32223.9%
More than 50 per cent apart56041.6%
More than 100 per cent apart31923.7%
'Actually paid' was negative1148.5%
'Actually paid' higher than the summary table62746.6%
'Actually paid' lower61345.5%
Identical1067.9%
The spread cuts both ways. Almost as many companies showed more pay actually paid as showed less, and 114 reported a negative figure, which happens when the value of earlier awards falls by more than the year's pay. Two numbers that move this differently, printed side by side, are what the proposal would collapse into one. The proposed Earned Compensation Table would count stock as earned when it vests and options when they are exercised, a third approach.
What else would change?
The list of disclosed executives would shrink. Named executive officers would be limited to the principal executive and principal financial officer, which the fact sheet says would cut the number "from typically five or more individuals to two officers in most circumstances". The threshold for itemising perquisites would rise fifteen-fold, and the guidance would lose its examples, "including security provided at an executive's personal residence or during personal travel".
Komposite's summary of the SEC's fact sheet for Release 33-11455.ItemTodayAs proposed
Named executive officersTypically five or morePrincipal executive and principal financial officer
Main pay tablesSummary Compensation Table and othersGranted, Earned and Status of Equity Awards tables
Pay versus performance'Compensation actually paid', five yearsEarned Compensation Table total, three years, shareholder return only
Perquisite threshold$10,000$150,000 per executive
Pay ratio median employeeAll employees worldwide, refreshed every three yearsUS full-time employees, every five years
The narrative section would get shorter too. The Compensation Discussion and Analysis would have to cover three topics: the objectives of the pay programme in relation to strategy, the material elements of pay and how they are set, and, where applicable, whether the latest say-on-pay vote was considered. The current rule's list of 15 example topics would go. Tables of what executives would receive in hypothetical terminations or changes of control would be replaced by a qualitative description of the material terms, and director pay disclosure would become, in the fact sheet's words, "more principles-based".
The proposal would also drop disclosure of risk-related pay policies and of equity grants made close to the release of material non-public information, and would let companies using long-form registration statements give pay data up to 120 days after year-end. The SEC has published the full proposing release.
The proposal is the latest of several this year that pare back disclosure rules. Komposite reported in September on the SEC's plans to rescind the shareholder-proposal rule and to scrap the pay-to-play rule for investment advisers. The comment period, once the Federal Register prints the release, will run for 60 days from that date.

# Margin debt slips 3.6 per cent from its June record

URL: https://kompositenews.com/markets/margin-debt-slips-3-6-per-cent-from-its-june-record/
Section: Markets
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-11-17T13:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-17T13:20:00Z

FINRA data show margin debt of $1.448tn in October 2026, 3.6% below June's $1.502tn record; the 49% rise into June was the steepest since 2007, by our count.

Investors owed their brokers $1.448tn in margin debt at the end of October 2026, 3.6 per cent less than the record $1.502tn of June, according to monthly figures that the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority posted on Friday.
The FINRA statistics count debit balances in customers' securities margin accounts at member brokers, money borrowed against shares and other securities. October's figure was down 2.1 per cent from September's $1.480tn and still 22.4 per cent higher than a year earlier, by our arithmetic. Free credit balances, the cash customers keep at brokers, were $210.3bn in cash accounts and $212.9bn in margin accounts. Netting both off the debit balance leaves $1.025tn of borrowing, up 29.7 per cent on October 2025.
Most of the rise came in three months. Debit balances grew 6.8 per cent in April, 8.5 per cent in May and 6.1 per cent in June, adding $281.2bn between March's $1.221tn and the June record, by our arithmetic. Margin debt had first passed its previous high, October 2021's $935.9bn, in January 2025. Free credit balances have grown far more slowly: up 6.2 per cent on the year in cash accounts and 9.0 per cent in margin accounts.
From FINRA's margin statistics; monthly changes are Komposite's arithmetic. Debit balances rose 22.6 per cent between December 2025 and June 2026.Month-endDebit balances ($bn)Change on the month
December 20251,225.6+0.9%
January 20261,279.0+4.4%
February1,253.2&minus;2.0%
March1,220.9&minus;2.6%
April1,304.3+6.8%
May1,415.6+8.5%
June1,502.1+6.1%
July1,417.2&minus;5.6%
August1,453.8+2.6%
September1,480.1+1.8%
October1,448.4&minus;2.1%
How unusual was the climb into June?
Steeper than before any peak in the series except those of 2000 and 2007. Komposite took FINRA's spreadsheet, which runs monthly from January 1997, and marked each month that was the highest within 18 months on either side. There are seven. Margin debt rose 49.0 per cent in the 12 months to June 2026, from $1.008tn in June 2025. The rise into March 2000 was 80.5 per cent and into July 2007 62.6 per cent. The rise into October 2021, the last peak before this one, was 41.9 per cent.
Komposite's analysis of FINRA's margin statistics, January 1997 to October 2026: debit balances in customers' securities margin accounts. A peak is the highest month within 18 months either side. Growth and falls are our arithmetic.Peak monthDebit balances ($bn)Growth in the 12 months into the peakLowest month in the next 12Fall to that low
March 2000299.9+80.5%March 2001&minus;41.7%
July 2007416.4+62.6%April 2008&minus;20.2%
April 2011360.9+22.1%September 2011&minus;17.3%
April 2015550.0+15.7%February 2016&minus;13.8%

October 2021935.9+41.9%October 2022&minus;30.6%
June 20261,502.1+49.0%July 2026 (so far)&minus;5.6%
After every earlier peak, debit balances fell at least 13.8 per cent within a year. After the 2000 and 2021 peaks they fell by more than 30 per cent. So far the drop from June has been smaller: the low was July's $1.417tn, 5.6 per cent below the record, and the figure climbed again in August and September before October's decline. Those six episodes are a small sample, and a peak can only be identified with hindsight; the table shows what followed, not what will follow.
Prices have not fallen much. The S&P 500 closed at 7,499.36 on 30 June and 7,580.07 on 30 October, a rise of 1.1 per cent, according to FRED, while margin debt fell 3.6 per cent over the same months. The index then lost 2.2 per cent to 7,416.59 by Monday's close. FINRA's November figure, which will show whether borrowing kept falling as prices did, is not due until next month.
What the figures do not show
FINRA's series covers member broker-dealers only. It does not include loans that banks make against securities, leverage inside funds, or the borrowing embedded in options and leveraged exchange-traded products. Debit balances also tend to rise with prices, because higher collateral values let investors borrow more against the same holdings. A drop of 3.6 per cent from the top is modest next to the falls in the table.
Why it matters: margin loans are callable, and when prices fall, brokers can demand more collateral or sell positions, which can add to the decline. The rise into June was large by the standards of the past 30 years, and the unwinding has been slow. Komposite has reported on other pockets of leverage this year, including the hedge-fund basis trade in Treasuries, and on bitcoin's November slide, during which the largest bitcoin fund shed 46m shares.

# Sixty-eight days to finish the upper C-band auction

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/sixty-eight-days-to-finish-the-upper-c-band-auction/
Section: Technology
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-11-17T13:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-17T13:00:00Z

FCC Auction 115 bidding starts 27 April 2027, 68 days before the statutory 4 July deadline; Auctions 107 and 110 took 71 and 91 days, by our count.

Bidding in the Federal Communications Commission's upper C-band auction opens on 27 April 2027, the FCC said on Friday, 68 days before the 4 July 2027 date by which Congress told it to finish.
The notice, DA 26-1219, sets the rules for Auction 115: 3,248 flexible-use licences covering 160 megahertz between 3.98 and 4.14 GHz, sold as eight 20-megahertz blocks in each partial economic area of the contiguous United States, with 15-year renewable terms. Applications open at noon Eastern time on 6 January and close at 18:00 on 20 January. Upfront payments are due by 18:00 on 18 March, a mock auction runs on 21 April and the first round follows six days later.
Where does the 4 July deadline come from?
From the budget law signed on 4 July 2025. The notice quotes Section 40002(b)(2) of Public Law 119-21, which directs the commission to "complet[e] a system of competitive bidding not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this Act for not less than 100 megahertz in the band between 3.98 gigahertz and 4.2 gigahertz." Auction 115 offers 160 megahertz, more than the floor. The law does not define "complete" in the passage the notice quotes, and the notice does not say which stage of the auction the agency treats as completion. The deadline falls on a Sunday.
The FCC's own record suggests the date will be tight if the auction runs at the pace of its predecessors. Komposite took the phase dates of the two most recent mid-band clock auctions from the agency's public reporting system. Auction 107, the first C-band sale, began on 8 December 2020; its clock phase ended on 15 January 2021 and its assignment phase, in which winners bid for specific frequencies, ended on 17 February, 71 days after the first round. Auction 110 took 91 days from first round to final assignment. The same spans counted from 27 April 2027 end on 7 July and 27 July.
Komposite's arithmetic from phase dates in the FCC's Auction Public Reporting System and the schedule in Public Notice DA 26-1219. Days are counted from the first day of bidding to the last day of the assignment phase. Past auctions are a guide to pace, not a forecast.AuctionBidding openedAssignment phase endedDaysSame length from 27 April 2027 ends
Auction 107 (3.7-3.98 GHz)8 Dec 202017 Feb 2021717 July 2027
Auction 110 (3.45-3.55 GHz)5 Oct 20214 Jan 20229127 July 2027
Auction 107, clock phase only8 Dec 202015 Jan 2021 (clock)384 June 2027
Auction 110, clock phase only5 Oct 202116 Nov 2021 (clock)428 June 2027
Statutory deadline for Auction 11527 Apr 2027684 July 2027
The clock phase alone would fit comfortably. Auction 107's took 38 days and Auction 110's 42, which from 27 April would end in early June. Auction 115 uses the same two-phase design, an ascending clock auction for generic blocks followed by an assignment phase, and the number of rounds a day is at the FCC's discretion. The notice declines a request from CTIA and Verizon to commit to "no fewer than four rounds per day", saying the agency will instead adjust the schedule, the activity requirement and the price increments "only as needed to bring the auction to a timely close".
Who asked for more time, and what did they get?
The carriers asked for a later start to the paperwork, not to the bidding. CTIA, the wireless trade group, AT&T and T-Mobile wanted the short-form deadline pushed back to shorten the quiet period during which applicants may not discuss bids, CTIA arguing that the industry was "just coming out of the quiet period for Auction 113". The notice declines, saying the schedule weighs "the statutory deadline for completing a system of competitive bidding" among other things. It designates AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon as nationwide providers for the anti-collusion rule, as in past auctions.
The money rules follow Auction 107 closely. Minimum opening bids are $0.03 per megahertz-pop in the 50 largest markets, $0.006 in the next 50 and $0.003 elsewhere, with a floor of $1,000 a block, the same tiers the FCC used in 2020. Upfront payments are roughly half the opening bids. There is no aggregate reserve price. The notice repeats that minimum bids "are not meant to predict the value of the spectrum". For scale only, Auction 107 raised $81.17bn in gross proceeds for 280 megahertz, by the FCC's figures, or about $290m a megahertz by our division; on top of their bids, Auction 115 winners must pay their share of the costs of moving satellite services out of the band, incentive payments to satellite operators that clear on time, and rebates for retrofitting aircraft radio altimeters, the notice says.
The July comment notice had proposed most of what Friday's notice adopts; comments closed on 24 August and replies on 8 September. Light Reading reported that the FCC expects the band to be "lit up for most Americans before the end of 2030". Komposite has covered the scramble for mid-band and low-band airwaves, including SpaceX's agreement to buy 800 MHz licences from Grain Management in October, and the FCC's equipment authorisation rule in September.
The next fixed date is the online application tutorial, due by 11 December, followed by the filing window 50 days from now. Whether the FCC can finish both phases in 68 days will be visible in the round schedule it publishes a week before bidding begins.

# The Entity List has not grown since October 2025

URL: https://kompositenews.com/policy/the-entity-list-has-not-grown-since-october-2025/
Section: Policy
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-11-14T14:20:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-14T14:20:00Z

BIS has added no one to the Entity List since 9 October 2025, 401 days, by our Federal Register count; Bessent said Commerce held up Megaspeed.

The Commerce Department has not added a single company or person to the Entity List, Washington's main export blacklist, since 9 October 2025, by Komposite's count of rules in the Federal Register. That is 401 days. On Friday the Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, said four other departments had wanted one company, Megaspeed, on the list "for months".
"Treasury, War, USTR and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months," Bessent said on CNBC's Squawk Box on Friday 13 November, according to the network's transcript. "But Commerce has the pin — Commerce BIS has the pin." The transcript's "pin" is the idiom Fortune and other outlets rendered as "pen": the Bureau of Industry and Security, part of Commerce, writes the list. "And you will have to ask them about their internal process," Bessent said.
Commerce has disputed a related account. Kristen Eichamer, a department spokeswoman, told Axios that Bessent and Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, had "no such conversation" about Megaspeed in the White House Situation Room, TNW reported, and an unnamed spokesperson told Semafor that "Treasury and Commerce have a great working relationship." Asked about the meeting on Friday, Bessent said: "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room." Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company, has said inspections found no evidence of violations, as Komposite has reported, and Nvidia barred sales and shipments to it in June 2025, according to a spokesman quoted by The Wall Street Journal.
How long has the list been frozen?
About twice as long as any earlier gap since 2018. Komposite searched all rules from the Bureau of Industry and Security that mention the Entity List and counted those whose titles announce additions. In every year from 2018 to 2024 there were between seven and 17. In 2025 there were six, the last on Thursday 9 October 2025, adding 29 entries covering 26 entities in China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates. In 2026 there have been none. The longest previous gap between such rules in our count was 196 days, from October 2018 to May 2019.
Komposite's count of rules from the Bureau of Industry and Security whose titles announce additions to the Entity List, from the Federal Register's own search of rules published since 1 January 2018. Corrections are excluded. Some sanctions rules have added names under other titles in past years, so earlier totals may be understated; none has done so since October 2025, by our check of all 16 BIS rules published since.YearFederal Register rules adding names to the Entity List
20188
20197
20208
202112
202211
202317
202411
20256 (the last on 9 October)
2026, to 14 November0
We also read every rule the bureau has published since 9 October 2025: 16, including a correction. None adds a name. Two take names off. A rule of 12 November 2025 removed one Chinese entity and six aliases of another, and a rule of 24 August 2026 removed one entity in Turkey, with a companion rule removing two Hong Kong addresses. The freeze is not a matter of one company; by our count no name of any kind has gone on the list in 13 months.
The dates line up awkwardly with the Megaspeed file. The last additions were published the day before Singapore's police confirmed, on 10 October 2025, that they were investigating Megaspeed, and four days before Senator Tom Cotton's letter of 13 October 2025 asked Lutnick to investigate it, as Komposite has reported. Nothing in the Federal Register since then mentions the company.
The last full year of additions was not small. The four rules published after the change of administration in January 2025 added 140 entities. One of them, the rule of 16 September 2025, included a single entity in Singapore among 32.
Komposite's compilation from the abstracts of each rule in the Federal Register. The four rules published after 20 January 2025 added 140 entities between them, by our addition.PublishedRuleNames addedWhere
16 Jan 20252025-0048016 entitiesBefore the change of administration
16 Jan 20252025-0070411 entitiesBefore the change of administration
28 Mar 20252025-0542670 entitiesChina and other destinations
28 Mar 20252025-0542712 entitiesChina and other destinations
16 Sep 20252025-1789332 entitiesChina 23, Turkey 3, UAE 2, India, Iran, Singapore and Taiwan 1 each
9 Oct 20252025-1950826 entities, 29 entriesChina 19, Turkey 9, UAE 1 (entries)
What does the trade truce have to do with it?
The pause began weeks before a deal with Beijing, and the deal froze a related rule. On 30 September 2025 the bureau published an interim rule under which any company at least 50 per cent owned by listed entities would automatically face the same restrictions, a standard it said was "designed to be consistent with longstanding Department of the Treasury practice". It was in force for 41 days. A White House fact sheet of 1 November 2025 said the United States would "suspend for one year, starting on November 10, 2025" that rule, as part of an agreement under which China would suspend rare-earth export controls "that it announced on October 9, 2025" — the same day as the last American additions.
The suspension rule said that "BIS will continue to evaluate U.S. national security and foreign policy interests related to these non-listed foreign affiliates of listed entities" and scheduled the 50 per cent rule to return on 10 November 2026. It did not return. A final rule published on Monday 9 November extends the suspension "through January 10, 2027", 62 days, and gives no reason. Its footer shows it was filed with the Federal Register at 4:15 p.m. on Thursday 5 November. The rule also misdates its subject: its background says the affiliates rule was published "On September 20, 2025", while the dates paragraph of the same rule, and the Federal Register itself, say 30 September.
Why would a listing matter for Megaspeed?
A listing turns a company into a licence requirement. The Export Control Reform Act, cited in this week's rule, authorises Commerce to maintain "a list of foreign persons and end uses that are determined to be a threat to the national security and foreign policy of the United States" and to restrict exports to them. Without a listing, suppliers rely on their own checks. Singapore's police have charged five people and six companies in a parallel server case, and the island's interior ministry said Washington had given "limited" help on Megaspeed, as Komposite reported in our timeline of that inquiry.
Megaspeed does not appear in American corporate disclosure at all. An SEC full-text search for the name across filings since January 2024 returns no results, by our check on Saturday, so no US-listed company has named it as a customer, supplier or risk. Bessent's broader complaint on Friday was about that gap. "I think there is a lot of leakage in the system and we are constantly working to close that down," he said, adding that chips had gone to "what were obviously pass-through shell companies".
Why it matters: the Entity List is the export system's most direct tool, and for 13 months it has not been used to add anyone, while the more automatic 50 per cent rule has been suspended as a bargaining chip with Beijing. Agencies that favour listing are now saying so in public, and the agency that decides has not explained its process. Earlier reporting set out how Commerce's own Megaspeed inquiry was paused at the Justice Department's request.
The next fixed dates are close. Nvidia reports results on Tuesday 17 November. Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on 10 December, Fortune reported. The suspension of the 50 per cent rule runs out on Sunday 10 January 2027, 57 days from now, unless Commerce extends it again.

# Microsoft moves its outage start six hours earlier

URL: https://kompositenews.com/technology/microsoft-moves-its-outage-start-six-hours-earlier/
Section: Technology
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-11-14T14:00:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-14T14:00:00Z

Microsoft's final record dates its 12-13 November 2026 Exchange Online outage from 10:05 to 16:10 GMT next day, 30h05m. Our SLA arithmetic.

Microsoft's closed record of this week's Exchange Online outage puts its start at 10:05 GMT on Thursday 12 November, six hours and 12 minutes earlier than the time the incident carried while it was open, and its end at 16:10 GMT on Friday 13 November. On those times the outage lasted 30 hours and 5 minutes.
The revised times appear in Microsoft's service-health record for incident EX1550543, as copied from the University of Pennsylvania's Microsoft 365 console, which marked it restored in a final update at 04:15 GMT on Saturday. The companion incident covering other Microsoft 365 services, MO1550821, was given the same start and end. When Komposite read the record on Friday, EX1550543 began at 16:17 GMT and MO1550821 at 18:26 GMT. Microsoft has not said why it moved the start.
For the first time Microsoft also gave a cause. "The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change," it wrote, first at 17:57 GMT on Friday and again in the final status. "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents." The same update apologised: "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused you and your business."
The SLA arithmetic, redone
The earlier start does not change the credit tier for a user who was out from beginning to end. Under Microsoft's Online Services service-level agreement, Exchange Online downtime is "Any period of time when users are unable to send or receive email with Outlook Web Access", and credits step up at 99.9, 99 and 95 per cent monthly uptime. Thirty hours and 5 minutes is 1,805 minutes, which leaves 95.82 per cent of a 30-day November, by our arithmetic. That is below 99 per cent, worth a 50 per cent credit on the month's Exchange Online fee, but above the 95 per cent line that would have meant a full refund.
Komposite's arithmetic on a 30-day month of 43,200 minutes, for a single user unable to send or receive mail in Outlook on the web for the whole period, using the times in Microsoft's service-health record and the tiers in its Online Services SLA. Microsoft measures downtime in user-minutes across a tenant, so most organisations will land in lower tiers.BasisMinutes outUptime for that user in NovemberCredit tier under the SLA
Start as first logged (16:17 GMT Thursday) to the final end time1,43396.68%Below 99%: 50% of the month's fee
Start as now recorded (10:05 GMT Thursday) to the final end time1,80595.82%Below 99%: 50% of the month's fee
Needed for the 100% tier (below 95%)2,16095.00%Would have required an outage until 22:05 GMT Friday
On Friday we calculated that a user out since the old start would cross the 95 per cent line at 04:17 GMT on Saturday if the outage continued. It did not; on the closed record the full-refund threshold would have needed the outage to last until 22:05 GMT on Friday. Microsoft's agreement also says credits are "your sole and exclusive remedy", and customers must claim them by the end of the month after the incident, so by 31 December for most monthly subscriptions.
Restored on paper, monitored for 12 hours
The recorded end time came before the updates stopped saying recovery was incomplete. At 20:02 GMT on Friday, almost four hours after the 16:10 end time, Microsoft wrote: "We do not have an ETA for full recovery yet. Service access can recover before mail flow fully normalizes." At 22:00 GMT it said: "Due to the severity of impact this incident caused, we're monitoring for an extended period." The final status came 12 hours after the recorded end. By our count, EX1550543 ran to 41 updates and MO1550821 to 37.
The final list of affected services is long. MO1550821's closing text names Exchange Online, the Microsoft 365 admin centre, Microsoft 365 apps, the Apps admin centre, Microsoft 365 Education, Copilot, Defender for Office 365, Defender XDR, Fabric, Graph, Intune, Planner and Power Apps among others, and repeats that "Elements of those services that do not depend on interaction with Exchange Online remained functional." For Copilot, Microsoft said users "may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses", and that its experiences may be unable to reach work email, calendars and files, a reminder of how much of the company's AI product depends on the mailbox.
Read together, the explanations have moved since Thursday. The early updates spoke of servers failing health checks and an overwhelmed connection process; early on Friday Microsoft said it was reverting "a recent network configuration change"; the final status links a recent change to an earlier capacity upgrade. That sequence is consistent with an investigation narrowing, but the final status is still labelled a "Preliminary root cause".
When does the full report arrive?
Microsoft's final status promises "a preliminary Post-Incident Report within two business days and a final Post-Incident Report within five business days". Counting from Friday's end, that means Tuesday 17 November and Friday 20 November, by our calendar. Microsoft's published service description is stricter on the first of those: a preliminary report "within 48 hours of incident resolution", which would have been 16:10 GMT on Sunday.
The report will be read for two things this record cannot answer: why the start moved to 10:05, more than six hours before the first public update at 16:20 GMT, and which customers and regions were affected in those hours. Komposite's account of the outage while it was running, and of how the SLA tiers apply, appeared on Friday. Organisations weighing how much mail to keep in a single provider's cloud have made different choices.

---

# The H200 licence rule, line by line

URL: https://kompositenews.com/ai/the-h200-licence-rule-line-by-line/
Section: AI
By: Komposite News Staff
Published: 2026-11-14T13:40:00Z
Updated: 2026-11-14T13:40:00Z

BIS's January 2026 rule lets H200 licences to China be reviewed case by case below 21,000 TPP and 6,500 GB/s. By our arithmetic the H200 is at 15,832.

The US rule that allows Nvidia's H200 to be licensed for China, published by the Commerce Department on 15 January 2026, does not name a ceiling by product. It sets two numbers: total processing performance below 21,000 and memory bandwidth below 6,500 gigabytes a second. By our arithmetic from Nvidia's own specifications, the H200 sits at 15,832 and 4,800, well inside both.
That detail matters after Friday. Scott Bessent, the Treasury Secretary, said on CNBC: "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any NVIDIA chips above H100s," according to the network's transcript. On the measure the rule uses for computing power, the H200 is not above the H100. The two chips have the same processing figures. What the H200 adds is memory: 141 gigabytes against 80, and 4.8 terabytes a second of bandwidth against 3.35, according to Nvidia's product pages.
What does the rule actually change?
It moves licence applications for chips under the two thresholds from a presumption of denial to case-by-case review when the buyer is in China or Macau. The rule names "the NVIDIA H200 or AMD MI325X" as examples. It is a review standard, not a general licence: every export still needs a licence from the Bureau of Industry and Security, and the bureau and other reviewing agencies decide each one.
The conditions are specific. The exporter must certify how many units have shipped in the United States, that exports will not delay American orders or divert foundry capacity from chips for American customers, and that "the aggregate shipments of the product to China and Macau will be no more than 50% of the total product shipped to customers for end use in the United States of that product". The buyer must run know-your-customer checks "to screen and prevent unauthorized remote access". Every shipment must be reviewed before export by "a qualified third-party testing lab" headquartered in the United States, which may test a sample from each batch. The applicant must also list remote users in Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Macau, North Korea, Russia and Venezuela.
The relaxation is narrower than its headline. It covers exports from the United States to buyers located in China or Macau. Re-exports from third countries keep the presumption of denial, and so do exports to companies headquartered, or with a parent headquartered, in Macau or a country in the group the regulations call D:5, which includes China, when the buyer is located somewhere else, such as a subsidiary in South-East Asia. The bureau classed the rule as "significant" under the executive order on regulatory review, and published it without prior notice or comment, which the export-control statute allows.
Komposite's arithmetic from Nvidia's published specifications for the H100, H200 and HGX B200. Nvidia quotes FP8 performance with sparsity; dense figures are half. Total processing performance (TPP) is dense operations per second times bit length, the measure in Export Control Classification Number 3A090. Bandwidths converted at 1 TB/s = 1,000 GB/s. Our figures are not an official classification.ChipDense FP8 (teraFLOPS)TPP, our arithmeticMemory bandwidth (GB/s)Inside the January rule's limits?
H100 SXM1,97915,8323,350Yes
H100 NVL1,670.513,3643,900Yes
H200 SXM1,97915,8324,800Yes
H200 NVL1,670.513,3644,800Yes
B200 (per GPU in an HGX B200)4,50036,000Not listedNo: TPP above 21,000
Rule's ceilingBelow 21,000Below 6,500
How do the chips compare with the thresholds?
The H200 uses about three-quarters of each allowance. Its total processing performance is 75 per cent of the 21,000 ceiling and its bandwidth 74 per cent of 6,500, by our division. The H100, at 3,350 gigabytes a second, uses about half the bandwidth allowance. Nvidia's Blackwell B200 is excluded on processing alone: at 4.5 petaFLOPS of dense FP8 per chip, half the sparse figure Nvidia publishes for an eight-chip HGX board, its total processing performance is about 36,000.
Total processing performance is the export-control measure of raw arithmetic: operations per second multiplied by the bit length of each operation. Nvidia's headline FP8 numbers assume sparsity, a technique that skips zeros, and the company states that dense performance is half. On dense figures, the H100 and H200 in their SXM form both come to 1,979 teraFLOPS of FP8, which gives 15,832.
Who holds the pen on licences?
Commerce. The rule was issued by the Bureau of Industry and Security, and Bessent made the same point about the separate question of blacklisting on Friday, saying that "Commerce BIS has the pin", as the CNBC transcript renders it. Commerce did not respond to Fortune's request for comment on his remarks. The rule itself expected modest use: the bureau estimated "100 more license applications per year" because "industry is more likely to submit licenses when there is a case-by-case review".
Use has been modest in Nvidia's accounts too. Its filing for the quarter to July recorded shipments under the H200 programme at less than 1 per cent of data-centre revenue, as Komposite reported in our reading of that 10-Q, and Beijing has restricted purchases by Chinese buyers. Enforcement has meanwhile become Washington's main tool, as we noted when export controls shifted from rulemaking to settlements.
The rule has been in force for 303 days, by our count. Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday 17 November, the first chance to see whether H200 shipments to China have moved from the margin of its accounts.
